planting.note: Plant container stock in fall into well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; island morning glory climbs by twining over a fence or trellis, or sprawls as a groundcover without one.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in well-drained soil; island morning glory is a woody-based perennial vine native to all the Channel Islands and the adjacent mainland coast from Monterey south into Baja California, producing funnel-shaped white-to-pink flowers over much of the year. It can climb to about 30 feet given support, or be left to sprawl as a dense groundcover on a dry slope. Once established it is drought-tolerant and needs little summer water, making it a good choice for a xeriscape or coastal garden wanting a long-blooming native vine.

planting.note: Plant rooted pad cuttings or container stock in spring into sharply drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; coastal cholla is cold-hardy to about 15°F once established.

directions: Plant in sharply drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; coastal cholla is a branching cactus found on all eight Channel Islands as well as the adjacent San Diego and Baja California mainland coast, growing to about 6 feet with showy magenta flowers in spring. It is cold-hardy to roughly 15°F once established and needs essentially no supplemental water beyond its first season. Handle with care when planting or maintaining, since the glochids (fine barbed spines) detach easily and embed readily in skin.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall into well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun along the coast or part shade inland; Channel Islands silverlace is rare in the wild but reasonably available from native-plant specialty nurseries.

directions: Plant in full sun along the coast or part shade inland, in well-drained, sandy or rocky soil; Channel Islands silverlace is an evergreen subshrub with finely divided, lacy, white-tomentose foliage native to coastal bluffs and cliffs of Santa Catalina, San Clemente, and Santa Barbara Island. Yellow summer flowers age to an attractive chocolate-brown, extending ornamental interest well past the main bloom period. Though rare in the wild, it is reasonably available from California native-plant specialty nurseries and is drought-tolerant once established, needing little water beyond the first season.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall into well-drained soil in full sun; this monotypic genus is a true San Clemente Island endemic, available through a small number of native-plant specialty sources.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; San Clemente Island chicory is the sole species in its genus, a shrubby composite endemic to San Clemente Island with pale pink-to-lavender, chicory-like flower heads. It is CNPS-ranked as rare but not federally or state listed, and is available through a small number of California native-plant specialty nurseries and botanic garden plant sales rather than general retail. Once established it is drought-tolerant, needing little water beyond its first growing season, and makes an interesting conversation-piece addition to a California native garden focused on island endemics.

planting.note: Plant container stock in fall into well-drained, sandy or rocky soil in full sun; this silver-leaved deerweed relative is a slope and bluff specialist suited to a dry California native garden.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy or rocky soil; Channel Islands silver deerweed is a silvery-leaved subshrub to about 2-3 feet, endemic to the Channel Islands and closely related to the mainland deerweed (Acmispon glaber). Yellow-to-orange pea-shaped flowers appear on the silvery foliage, drawing pollinators to a drought-tolerant slope or bluff planting. It needs little water once established and pairs well with other Channel Islands endemics in a dedicated island-native garden bed.
